```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_scip <- requireNamespace("scip", quietly = TRUE)
has_osqp <- requireNamespace("osqp", quietly = TRUE)
has_nloptr <- requireNamespace("nloptr", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(optcompR)
```

optcompR describes an optimization problem once, as variables, expressions,
constraints and an objective, and then classifies it, chooses a capable solver
With several objectives there is usually no single best point, only a set of
Pareto optimal points where no objective can improve without another getting
worse. optcompR offers three scalarizations. Each restores the model's own
objective and removes temporary constraints afterwards.

```{r}
m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", lower = 0, upper = 4)
y <- opt_variable(m, "y", lower = 0, upper = 4)
opt_constraint(m, x + y >= 4)
cost <- 2 * x + y
risk <- x + 3 * y
```

## Weighted sums

```{r}
r <- opt_weighted(m, list(cost = cost, risk = risk), weights = c(1, 1))
r$objective_values
```

Weighted sums with positive weights give Pareto optimal points, but only
supported ones: points on nonconvex parts of the front (and many points of
integer problems) are never reached.

## Lexicographic order

```{r}
st <- opt_lexicographic(m, list(cost = cost, risk = risk))
st[[2]]$objective_values
opt_value(st[[2]], c(x, y))
```

Cost is optimized first; risk is then minimized among points whose cost is
within a relative tolerance `tol` of the best.

## Epsilon constraints and the Pareto front

```{r}
front <- opt_epsilon_constraint(m, cost, risk, epsilon = seq(4, 12, by = 2))
front
plot(front$secondary, front$primary, type = "b",
     xlab = "risk", ylab = "cost", main = "Pareto front")
```

Epsilon constraints reach every Pareto point, including unsupported ones,
but can return weakly Pareto optimal points when the bound on the secondary
objective is not tight.
